title: Laminar flame speed against equivalence ratio: does the model match flame data?
summary: A bell-shaped curve of unstretched flame speed over fuel-air ratio, with experiment markers and error bars, one curve per dilution level. It shows where a model is fast, slow, or peaks in the wrong place.

media.alt: Line plot of laminar flame speed against equivalence ratio with three dilution levels, curves for a model and open markers with error bars for experiment.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does it match flame data?
read_the_figure.axes: x: equivalence ratio phi (dimensionless; 1 is stoichiometric, left lean, right rich). y: laminar flame speed S_L in cm/s on a linear axis.
look_at: Where is the peak in phi, and does the model peak where the markers peak?
Do the open markers scatter on both sides of each curve, within their error bars?
How much does each dilution level lower the whole curve?
Is the gap between model and data larger at the lean or the rich edge?
read_the_figure.proves: A model whose curve runs through the markers for all dilution levels reproduces the speed of the flame as the mixture changes, not only at one composition. It does not prove the chemistry is right: speed is one global target.
if_wrong: Peak shifted to the right or left of the data: the fuel's diffusion or the rich-side chemistry is off.
Markers systematically above the curve on one flank: the model under-predicts speed in that regime.
Initial temperature, pressure or dilution missing: flame speed depends strongly on all three, so the curve cannot be compared.

terms.meaning: Speed at which an unstretched, planar, adiabatic premixed flame front moves into the cold unburnt gas. A property of the mixture, not of the burner.
Actual fuel-to-oxidiser ratio divided by the stoichiometric one. 1 is exact, below 1 lean, above 1 rich.
Replacing part of the mixture by an inert such as nitrogen. It lowers flame temperature and speed.
The stated measurement uncertainty on a marker, usually one standard uncertainty (state it).
Corrected to zero flame stretch: experiments extrapolate to this, models compute it directly.

remember: Open markers are experiment, lines are model. Same colour means same dilution.
Peak flame speed for most hydrocarbons and hydrogen sits slightly rich of phi = 1.
S_L is a scalar of the mixture at stated T and p (here 300 K, 1 atm), in cm/s or m/s.
Dilution lowers the curve without moving the peak much.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along x encodes phi, position along y encodes S_L. Colour and line style (solid, dashed, dash-dot) separate dilution levels, and marker shape repeats that choice so colour is not the only cue. Open markers with vertical bars are measurements; continuous lines are the model. Two kinds of mark for two kinds of evidence.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A flame speed is a function of one composition variable at fixed T and p. The natural picture is a curve of speed against phi: it has a peak, two flanks and a lean and rich limit, and the experimental points are few. Showing curve and points together lets the eye judge agreement across the whole flammable range. Thermal flame theory says S_L scales as the square root of thermal diffusivity times a chemical rate, so anything that lowers flame temperature, such as dilution, lowers the curve in a smooth, comparable way.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Where is the peak for 0 percent dilution? The solid teal curve tops out near phi = 1.07 at roughly 39 cm/s, slightly rich. Q2: By how much does 20 percent dilution lower the peak? The dash-dot amber curve peaks near 25 cm/s, which is 25/39 = 0.65 of the undiluted value, a 35 percent drop. Q3: Where do the markers and the model disagree most? At the rich end, phi = 1.5 on the undiluted series, where the marker is near 18 cm/s while the curve is about 16, and again at phi = 0.71, where the marker sits above the line. Both are within a couple of error bars, so the model is acceptable but slightly low on the flanks.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Dilution labelled: the legend and title state 0, 10 and 20 percent N2 and the initial state T = 300 K, p = 1 atm. Without them the curves are not a comparison, because every unlabelled parameter (T, p, dilution) moves the whole curve.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A linear axis makes the peak region look important and hides the flammability limits, where the speed falls to a few cm/s and relative errors are largest. Error bars that are small compared to the model-to-model spread give a false sense of validation, and extrapolation of stretched flames to zero stretch adds systematic error that bars do not show. A model that agrees at 1 atm may fail at 10 atm.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A residual plot of (model minus experiment) over S_L against phi isolates the error. A table with the same data is exact. For many conditions, a parity plot of model against experiment collapses the composition axis. For pressure dependence use S_L against p on log axes.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a lower residual strip that shares the x axis, mark the stoichiometric line phi = 1, and draw a shaded band for the experimental scatter of one reference dataset.

steps.title: Equivalence ratio from a composition
steps.note: The stoichiometric ratio comes from 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O.

steps.title: Thermal-theory scaling of flame speed
steps.note: Mallard and Le Chatelier scaling: a four-fold change in the chemical rate gives a two-fold change in speed. Dilution cuts the flame temperature, and the rate falls steeply with it.

worked.title: Dilution effect and phi of an H2-air mixture
worked.problem: A premixed H2-air mixture has 29.6 percent H2 by mole in air (21 percent O2, 79 percent N2). Find phi. Then, from the reference render, find the ratio of the 20 percent-diluted peak to the undiluted peak.

solution.text: Moles of O2 per mole of mixture: air fraction 0.704 times 0.21 = 0.1479.
Peaks read off the render: 39 and 25.3 cm/s.

worked.answer: phi is about 1.00 (stoichiometric); the 20 percent-diluted peak is 65 percent of the undiluted one.

analyze.q: Which series is best reproduced by the model, and what feature of the figure tells you?
analyze.hint: Compare marker positions relative to the line.

analyze.q: The model peaks at phi = 1.07 and the data seem to peak at 1.05. Is that a real discrepancy?
analyze.hint: Compare to the width of the error bars and the spacing of the markers.

evaluate.q: Is agreement at 300 K and 1 atm enough to trust the model inside an engine?
evaluate.hint: Which parameter does the figure not vary?

checks.q: What do the open markers and the lines stand for?
checks.answer: Open markers are experiments with error bars, lines are the model, one colour per dilution.

checks.q: The undiluted peak is 39 cm/s. Thermal theory says S_L goes as the square root of the rate. By what factor must the rate fall to give 25 cm/s?
checks.answer: (25/39)^2 = 0.41: the rate falls by about 59 percent.

checks.q: Experiment markers sit above the model on both flanks but on the peak. What could cause that, and what would you check?
checks.hint: Think about stretch correction and measurement uncertainty at the flammability limits.
checks.answer: Flame speed is hardest to measure near the limits, where stretch and buoyancy corrections are large, or the model's low-temperature chemistry is slow. Check the extrapolation method and the error bars before changing the mechanism.
